issues.legal_issue: A party cannot challenge an adoption’s validity on a ground that was not pleaded when the issue was not tried and the parties had no opportunity to lead evidence on it.
material_facts: The defendants did not plead that the adoptive father lacked power to adopt the adopted person because he was the adoptive father’s daughter’s son.
The validity of the adoption was therefore not in issue, and the parties had no opportunity to lead evidence on that question.
issues.conclusion: The defendants could not challenge the validity of the adoption on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: A ground that was not pleaded and was not put in issue cannot be raised where the parties consequently had no opportunity to adduce evidence on it. The judgment cited no earlier case or statutory provision for this ruling.

predicates.adoption_succession_dispute: The parties are litigating succession in reliance on an adoption.
predicates.invalidity_ground_not_pleaded: The party challenging the adoption did not plead the ground on which it later seeks to dispute the adoption’s validity.
predicates.no_opportunity_to_lead_evidence_on_valid: Because the validity ground was not in issue, the parties had no opportunity to lead evidence on it.

issues.definition: When an adoption-based succession dispute involves an unpleaded validity ground that the parties had no opportunity to address with evidence, a challenge to the adoption’s validity on that ground is barred.

issues.legal_issue: Under the applicable customary law, only a formal adoption that completely transfers the adopted person from the natural family to the adoptive family gives a right to collateral succession in the adoptive family; a customary appointment of an heir does not.
material_facts: The adopted person was adopted under the customary law governing the parties, and his descendants claimed through him a right to succeed collaterally in the adoptive family.
The courts below found that the adoption was a customary appointment of an heir rather than a formal adoption, and the evidence supported that finding.

After the adoption, the adopted person succeeded to property left by his natural brother and by a collateral relative in his natural family, indicating that he retained collateral succession rights in that family.
The claimed succession to property associated with the adoptive family was consistent with an appointed heir’s succession to the adoptive father’s property and did not establish a formal adoption.
The claimants bore the burden of proving that the adoption was formal and effected a complete change in family; the record did not establish that change.
issues.conclusion: The adoption was only a customary appointment of an heir. The adopted person therefore had no right to succeed collaterally in the adoptive family and was not a preferential heir to the deceased’s property; the appeal was allowed and the suit was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Article 49 of Rattigan’s Digest of Customary Law: without formal adoption, the relationship is personal and the appointed heir does not acquire collateral succession rights in the adoptive family. Articles 52 and 54 recognize that an appointed heir may succeed to the adoptive father’s property and that his male issue may succeed after him. A formal customary adoption severs collateral succession rights in the natural family and confers them in the adoptive family; Hindu-law rituals are not required. Whether an adoption is formal is a question of fact, and loss of natural-family collateral rights is strong evidence of a complete transfer, while their retention indicates an informal appointment. The court relied on the Riwaj-i-am, whose entries are presumed correct and normally prevail over a conflicting general digest as to local custom, read in light of judicial decisions. It cited Jai Kaur v. Sher Singh and Salig Ram v. Munshi Ram on the Riwaj-i-am; Mela Singh v. Gurdas on customary appointment of an heir; Abdur Rehman v. Raghubir Singh and Waryaman v. Kanshi Ram on formal customary adoption; and Teju v. Kesar Singh and Teja Singh v. Kesar Singh on collateral succession following formal adoption.

predicates.customary_adoption_succession_dispute: The dispute concerns a claimed right of collateral succession based on an adoption governed by customary law.
predicates.retained_collateral_rights_in_natural_fa: After the adoption, the adopted person succeeded to property through collateral relations in the natural family, indicating that he retained collateral succession rights there.
predicates.no_proof_of_complete_family_transfer: The party claiming through the adopted person did not establish a clear transfer that ended his natural-family membership and collateral rights and made him a member of the adoptive family with collateral rights there.

issues.definition: In a customary adoption-based collateral succession dispute, retained collateral rights in the natural family together with no proof of a complete family transfer means that the adopted heir has no collateral succession right in the adoptive family.
